event: VXE-815 transitioned to hover for a VTOL landing but could not descend for about 15 to 18 minutes in strong wind; the operator washed off height manually and landed safely.
component: wind generated wing lift during VTOL hover
failure_mode: wing lift from strong wind and updrafts at a cliff-top landing site exceeded aircraft weight so the lift motors ran at their lower limit and the aircraft could not descend
contributing: operating outside wind limits
light aircraft with high aspect ratio wing
cliff-top landing site with vertical air currents
manual had no caution or procedure for excess lift during descent

evidence.quote: It is holding station in VTOL with motors bouncing off the rails low
Additionally, there appears to be a significant amount of wind, which may have generated a lot of lift preventing the system from descending
this is backed up with low power-draw on the lift battery and the vertical lift motors being seen to start/stop whilst in the hover

reasoning: Log review shows the lift motors sitting at their lower limit while holding station and low HLB power draw, which means the wing was carrying the aircraft. The operator report on the linked ticket describes moderate on-shore wind at a cliff-top site and lift motors starting and stopping. The aircraft behaved as designed in an out-of-limit wind condition.
notes: VXEP-1570 is a second ticket for the same VXE-815 event (same AAR file) and carries the manual-update corrective action. Eric Brewer also noted the altitude above takeoff point went negative, either terrain or a GPS altitude error; not pursued. The CLIMB ABORT LIFT SYSTEM FAULT caption in VXEP-1570 was not explained further.

event: USASOC VXE-525 nosedived into the ground from about 800 ft AGL right after releasing one of two wing-mounted FPV drones from the wing utility pylon, damaging the center panel, a tail boom and the right wing.
contributing: about 3 lb FPV drone on each wing plus HD40 payload, above the 2 lb Payload ICD limit
asymmetric load after releasing only one of two drones
no weight or size limits for the wing utility pylon in the supplement

evidence.quote: Then there is a big jump when the munition was dropped, which would imply that the placement of the mass was not near the Xcg of the aircraft.
that FDR appears to show just a normal VTOL landing.
The corresponding xcomm log also shows vtol throttles at beginning and end of log file (indicating normal VTOL landing).
The only place with weight constraints is the Payload ICD which states 2lbs

team_view_in_comments: Then there is a big jump when the munition was dropped, which would imply that the placement of the mass was not near the Xcg of the aircraft.

would_settle_it.what: the FDR covering the drop event itself (the reviewed FDR00123 shows only a normal VTOL landing)

would_settle_it.file: customer flight data for the drop flight
would_settle_it.what: logs that can be correlated to the drop time, plus photos of the damage and drone mounting orientation

reasoning: The first log reading suggested an off-CG mass release, but a later review found the FDR used showed only a normal VTOL landing and the XCOMM log also showed a normal landing. No data from the actual drop was identified, so the cause cannot get past the symptom. The loading (about 3 lb per wing) was above the 2 lb ICD limit, which is a plausible contributor but not shown to be the cause.
notes: Description is inconsistent on altitude (3k out, 800 ft AGL) and on the number of drones carried and dropped. Engineers questioned the customer statement on damage. Ticket was effectively left awaiting correct data.

event: During a high density altitude flight at Enterprise, Oregon, the aircraft at about 14,000 ft MSL in strong winds aloft showed a pitch oscillation, stopped tracking its orbit and then did a Low Energy auto RTB.
failure_mode: flight in winds aloft above 40 kt (out of spec) at very high altitude degraded pitch control and orbit tracking and consumed energy, triggering Low Energy auto RTB
contributing: very high density altitude (about 14,000 ft MSL)
0.1 Hz fixed wing log rate too slow for controls analysis

evidence.quote: Further the winds were > 40Kts aloft in the data which is out of spec.
the data rate in a nominal data log is only 0.1Hz during fixed wing operation, which is too slow to perform a controls performance analysis of dynamic behavior.
the plane exhibited a pitch oscillation and stopped tracking the orbit accurately
Customer operating outside of aircraft limitations, and provided them with answers to questions

team_view_in_comments: Customer operating outside of aircraft limitations

would_settle_it.what: high-rate attitude and control data, if any, around the pitch oscillation

reasoning: The data showed winds aloft above 40 kt, outside the aircraft limit, at the time the oscillation and poor orbit tracking appeared. The nominal 0.1 Hz fixed wing log rate is too slow to analyze the oscillation itself, so the control mechanism is not confirmed. The evidence narrows the event to flight outside the wind envelope.
notes: Title says VXE-790, the tail field says VXE-709; VXEP-1484 says the Enterprise team moved to backup airframe 709, so 709 is used. The Low Energy RTB was a designed response. Closed as Won't Do.

event: VXE-697 at Enterprise, Oregon aborted its VTOL launch on a low climb rate abort after the VTOL autopilot barometer pressure reading had dropped to zero; no damage beyond scratches.
component: VTOL AP barometer (U11) or its interface resistors R97, R98, R99
failure_mode: barometric pressure read as zero (flagged bad in SensorBaro), corrupting derived airspeed and density and causing a low climb rate launch abort
contributing: no operator warning when baro was flagged bad
VTOL AP baro not calibrated or range-checked in the electronics shop
legacy use of VTOL board baro instead of ADP
removed VTOL boards scrapped before investigation

evidence.quote: The baro pressure from the internal sensor goes to zero and then derivative data is not usable.
[21:20:31.618 1566.618] DebugMsg Climb abort, low climb rate
This data comes from the barometer on the VTOL board, not the ADP.
The VTOL AP and INT boards were replaced to verify that the issue was isolated to those assemblies.
Component failure.  Either U11, the supply voltage through the resistor R97, or SCLK and SDI resistors R98 and R99.

team_root_cause:
Inconclusive.  Faulty component highly suspected. Unable to confirm since the removed electronics were scrapped. 

While corrupted firmware or a faulty microcontroller cannot be ruled out, only the pressure data was misreported; airspeed and density values were secondary calculations derived from the barometric measurement. This makes a barometer component failure the most likely root cause. Alternatively, the issue may have originated from passive components associated with the barometer interface, such as the supply-voltage resistor (R97) or the SCLK and SDI series resistors (R98 and R99).

would_settle_it.what: inspect U11 barometer and R97, R98, R99, reflash to rule out firmware; board was scrapped so this cannot now be done

reasoning: Log data shows the VTOL board barometer pressure going to zero with repeated baro jump warnings before the low climb rate abort. Replacing the VTOL AP and INT boards cleared the fault and the aircraft flew twice normally, which isolates the fault to those boards. The removed boards were scrapped, so the barometer IC, its series and supply resistors, the microcontroller and firmware corruption all remain possible.
notes: Swap test replaced the VTOL AP and INT boards together. The last comment says a baro fix was included in software 6.7.1, which suggests software handling of a bad baro was also changed. The route and landing pattern JSON attachments hold no fault data.

event: VXE-499 (Riga FLOPS) aborted its VTOL launch about 5 to 10 seconds after takeoff and landed hard after HLB cell 2 dropped to zero.
failure_mode: cell voltage dropout to zero under launch load
contributing: part of the systemic HLB cell failure investigation (VXEP-1449), where dissection found electrolyte leaking or evaporating in the Advanced Energy cells
battery storage history unknown

evidence.quote: I reviewed the data and found that cell 2 on the HLB dropped to Zero.
Approximately 5-10 seconds into launch, launch was abort
Battery Dissection led to discovery of leaking / evaporating electrolyte material inside the 3300mAh Advanced Energy Cells within the HLB.

would_settle_it.what: HLB cell voltage plot showing cell 2 dropping to zero during launch
DCIR test and dissection of cell 2 to confirm the cell-level mechanism

reasoning: The flight data review found HLB cell 2 dropping to zero during launch, which explains the abort and hard landing. The battery was quarantined and rolled into the master HLB ticket, where dissection of other failed packs found electrolyte loss in the cells; this pack itself was not dissected, so the cell-level mechanism is not confirmed.
notes: The mishap form attachment is a blank template. The GCS event log attached to VXEP-1489 covers this 22 Aug 12:30 flight: launch detected then landing detected 28 seconds later with fault status 0x14014000. The master ticket is VXEP-1449, reached through VXEP-1413.

event: VXE-499 (Riga training asset) failed to start its VTOL motors at the transition point on landing after an abort and second approach, kept descending and crashed in a field near the GCS; the aircraft was replaced.
failure_mode: lift bus voltage sagged with almost no current drawn when VTOL throttles were commanded at transition, pointing to a high resistance in the HLB power path
contributing: Activate User Landing Control did not populate until on the ground
slow launch with long pause at 20 ft earlier in the flight
aircraft did not hold altitude after Orbit Here Now command

evidence.quote: It appears to be a power issue, throttle commands are sent on VTOL transition, voltage sags but no current is pulled.
There is no indication of a HLB cell issue.
A large voltage drop with a small amount of current indicates a resistance issue (likely AS150 contact).
The VTOL motors did not initiate and the vehicle flew past the point.
Time: 081:00.843  Fault Status Changed: 0x000B4080

team_view_in_comments: It appears to be a power issue, throttle commands are sent on VTOL transition, voltage sags but no current is pulled.

would_settle_it.what: HLB voltage and current at the VTOL transition, size of the sag versus current
contact resistance measurement and visual check of the AS150 contacts and HLB connector
ESC and lift bus data at the transition point

reasoning: Log review found that the VTOL throttles were commanded at transition but the lift bus voltage sagged while almost no current flowed, and no HLB cell problem was seen. A voltage drop with little current points to a series resistance in the power path, and the plan names the AS150 contact as the likely spot. No resistance measurement or inspection was recorded before the aircraft was replaced, so this stays a narrowed, low confidence result.
notes: The GCS event log was searched by session; the crash flight is the 28 Aug 11:38 session (pack T95_V499_250828_123718) showing RTB, abort, Orbit Right Here Now, fault status 0x000B4080 and landing detected 3 s later. RMA-796 intake PDF has no text and the RMA ended in a full aircraft replacement without teardown findings. HLB 2-2198 on this flight differs from the HLB in VXEP-1485.

event: VXE-732 could not hold 250 m route or 220 m loiter orbits and flew wide landing patterns during flight testing because its airspeed reading was wrong.
failure_mode: airspeed calibration low, so the aircraft flew at a much higher true ground speed than intended and could not turn tight enough for the commanded orbit radius
contributing: wind on the ground during the pitot press calibration
winds aloft

evidence.quote: It was noted that the aircraft reported high ground speeds but airspeed plus wind speed did not equal ground speed.
Looking at the airspeed it seems like there is more wind on the ground being picked up after the pitot press.
There appears to be an airspeed calibration issue on this vehicle.
The minimum radius would need to be increased with a ground speed that high.
Post flight inspection of the ailerons and servos noted no issues.

team_root_cause: Airspeed calibration was incorrect leading to poor lateral tracking and difficulty maintaining the desired radius of the loiter. Winds would be a complicating factor.

would_settle_it.what: airspeed versus ground speed comparison showing the calibration error

reasoning: Reported ground speed (67 mph) was far above airspeed plus wind (37 plus 6 mph) with light surface wind, which shows the airspeed reading was wrong. Engineers saw wind on the ground picked up after the pitot press calibration and confirmed an airspeed calibration error. Ailerons and servos were inspected with no issues, and the flight dynamics engineer agreed the high ground speed explains the large orbit radius.
notes: Two early comments hold embedded files not matched to attachments. The calibration cause (wind during pitot press) is inferred from one comment.

event: HLB SN 2-4867 for aircraft 826 was found with cell 6 at 2.95 V against 3.3 to 3.4 V on the other cells when checked during EMC testing; no flight was involved.
failure_mode: low cell voltage (self discharge of one cell)
contributing: a second HLB from the same kit HLBCK-413 and same date of manufacture (VXEP-1495) also had cell 6 low with no cycles, suggesting a production lot issue

evidence.quote: Cell 6 shows 2.95V, other cells 3.3-3.4V using HLB battery checker
has cell 6 at 2.78V remaining cells 3.3-3.4V per HLB battery checker
No battery cycles, pulled straight from production HLB kit
placed in yellow fire cabinet engineering upper shelf 9/3/25

would_settle_it.what: DCIR and self-discharge test and dissection of cell 6 to find why it lost charge
the battery data from the EMC test the reporter was asked to add

reasoning: A battery checker measurement shows cell 6 well below the other cells, which pins the fault to that cell. A second pack from the same kit and build date had the same cell 6 low with no cycles, which points to the cells or pack build rather than use. event: Edge-owned VXE-863 on loan to CBP showed AGL higher than actual, sharp nose-down pitches about 8 minutes in, and a very slow VTOL descent from about 300 ft during landing in light rain over mountainous terrain; it landed safely.
failure_mode: baro altitude calibration reset mid flight, so the aircraft thought it was lower than it was and used a slow descent setpoint during VTOL landing
contributing: light drizzle during flight
steep mountainous terrain
moisture seen in LRF lens (judged not a factor)

evidence.quote: Baro Altitude appears to have had its calibration adjusted mid flight around where there were some altitude disturbances.
It is likely that the vehicle thought it was lower to the ground because of the baro cal reset, which would have resulted in a lower vertical speed setpoint.
Replacement ADP sent out and replaced on 9/30/2025. Flight anomalies were resolved.
The LRF data looks normal

team_view_in_comments: Replaced ADP and flight anomalies went away.

would_settle_it.what: baro altitude trace showing the mid-flight calibration change
check baro sensor and moisture ingress in the removed ADP

reasoning: Log review found the baro altitude calibration changed mid flight where the altitude disturbances occurred, which explains the wrong AGL and the slow descent. LRF data looked normal. Replacing the ADP cleared the anomalies, a swap test that points to the ADP, though the removed unit was not inspected and the reason for the calibration change was never found.
notes: The nose-down pitches and a loss of link after a simulation were reported but not separately explained. VXEP-220 was mentioned and ruled unrelated by engineering; not read.
